excerpt: Youth recruiting used to run on who you knew and what you could pay for. AI is changing the price of getting noticed, and the platforms racing to own that relationship have not settled who wins.
A franchise that finished 11-33 now holds the most valuable asset in women's basketball: the No. 1 pick, one season after it existed.
You cannot buy the Sandy Liang Formula 1 collection unless you carry an American Express card, which makes the merchandise a membership benefit as much as a product.
The NFL and the Bundesliga renewed a deal with no price tag, and the trade is easy to read: one league lends its stadiums, the other borrows its stage.
Bluestone's first buyout is not a team, a league or a streaming service. It is a fabrication shop that builds the sets people walk into.
Yamaha is paying about 3.6 times sales for a business whose revenue shrank last year, and the reason is on every stage Disguise touches.
Every match in a volleyball league uses the same piece of equipment, which makes the ball the cheapest media asset a sponsor can own.
Barcelona's latest financing is two different problems solved with two different instruments, and the club's total debt now sits at 2.68 billion euros.
The BBC built a second screen that lives inside the first one, and now it wants to sell it to the broadcasters it competes with.
WeTheHobby, the Rochester based live selling and card breaking company, is looking for a full time, on-site On-Air Personality to become the face of the brand.
The Ducks dropped the Mighty Ducks name in 2006. Twenty years later, fans spent an estimated half a million dollars in a day on a jersey that brings it back.
Golfers have been settling five dollar Nassau matches in the parking lot for a century. Lucra and Barkie.ai want to turn that handshake into a payments product.
RedBird Capital Partners is no longer managing a soccer club in Milan. It is building a city platform, and it hired a conference commissioner to run it.
In an NBA locker room, the person who decides what goes in a player's shoe is often the athletic trainer, and Move Insoles has signed up the association that represents them.
Washington did not sell its stadium name for a record total. It sold it for a record annual rate, and the shorter term is what makes that possible.
Thibaut Courtois did not buy a padel club or a player. He backed the company that runs the tournament, which is where a lot of padel's value currently sits.
Mike Repole has not bought Spezia yet, and the gap between the announcement and the approval is the part worth watching.
The pro shop is one of the last places in a racquet club where revenue still gets tracked on a clipboard, and CourtReserve has bought its way into it.
A sponsorship that began as a payments deal is now a three category partnership. UEFA and Ant Group have renewed through EURO 2028, bringing the relationship to ten years.
Most card companies chase the star. ONIT is betting that the roster is the product.
Before a high school league plays a full season, it has already decided who controls the data on its players.

The most interesting part of the new Bears pitch in Chicago is not the $10 billion. It is the offer to buy the team's Arlington Heights land, which targets what the developers call the key impediment to keeping the stadium in the city.
A $625 million enterprise value for the San Jose Earthquakes says as much about the stadium as it does about the team.
TMRW Sports is hiring a Chief Financial Officer in Orlando, a finance role that spans three leagues and whatever the company builds next.
CAA is hiring an Associate in Strategic Development focused on ventures, CPG and consumer brands, based in Los Angeles.
Fanatics Live is turning celebrity collectors into programming, and its channel list is starting to look like a talent roster.
Novig is hiring a Head of Business Development in New York, and the job sits at the center of how a prediction market gets its prices.
The strongest number behind the Pro Climbing League's £3.2 million seed round is not on the cap table. It is 4,000 tickets sold on the first day of sales for a season that has not started.

The PEAKCONF | SportsTech Conference Startup World Cup opens its 2027 qualifying rounds this week with a Fan Tech Qualifier on Thursday, November 19 at 12PM CET, hosted by Profluence Sports and SportsTechX.
Euroleague Basketball is moving to fill its next four seats before the NBA has finished building a rival, and the six clubs at the front of the line say a lot about where the league wants to grow.
MotoGP has changed American broadcasters so often that the most valuable part of the ESPN deal may be that it stays put.

The headline number in digital card rips is $2 billion. The number that explains why gambling companies are crowding in is smaller: Bank of America estimates operators keep at least 6% of what users spend.
Athlete-backed funds usually lead with a famous name. Athletic Ventures is leading with something less glamorous: a distribution network for startups.
Canada's answer to a disappointing Winter Olympics is to put most of the new money into getting more people to play, not into winning more medals.
College sports has debated for years whether athletes can bargain collectively. Tennessee's men's basketball players answered a narrower and more useful question: what would the deal actually say?
The lawyers who price sports deals are moving to firms built for the buyers now writing the checks.
Tom Brady is leaving Birmingham City at the moment the club he backed has reached the top of English football's second tier.
Horse racing has produced plenty of plans to modernize the sport. Few came from an executive who spent years running the company that owned Formula 1.
Most venues know how many tickets they sold. Few know where those fans stood, what they bought, or which part of the concourse nobody walked through.
A record month for New York sports betting did not turn into a record month for the state's budget.
The person who built Boardroom's brand partnerships, events and print magazine now runs the company.
Related Companies president Bruce Beal called a favorite stadium assumption a fallacy: build the stadium, and everything around it does not automatically get better.
The next round of MLB's labor fight could turn on two legal moves, and neither has happened yet.
Major League Soccer had a World Cup year, Lionel Messi's traveling show and an attendance gain of 0.3%.
John Malone gave up voting control of Liberty Media without selling to an outsider. He swapped his way out.
The first union for a major U.S. sports league's digital staff arrives weeks before the league's own labor fight.
Otro Capital paid about $200 million for 24% of Alpine's Formula 1 team in 2023. It is now exploring a sale at valuations that look very different.

The grand prize at IBM's Sports Tech Startup Challenge is not a check. It is up to $100,000 toward a proof of concept with IBM's Sports and Entertainment Partnerships Team, plus up to $20,000 in IBM credits.
Some college fans want the picture from the national TV broadcast and the voice of their own radio announcers. Homestream is building a business around giving them both.
A youth basketball media company is sponsoring a fifth-grade team for a second year, and the sponsorship doubles as a content engine.
Following women's sports should not take five apps, three group chats and a good memory. SheScores is built around a simple idea: put every game in one place.
Fast-growing leagues eventually need an unglamorous layer: an agreed way to count the game. The ECAC has picked its answer for women's flag football.
The PWHL has named its four expansion teams, but fans will not see those names on a jersey until next season.
Golden State won a WNBA title in its second season, which raises a sponsorship question: what does a championship add to a book that was already full?
Twelve percent of Atlanta Braves Holdings' revenue produced more adjusted profit than the entire company reported.
The headline number on ESPN's new College Football Playoff deal overstates what ESPN is adding, and the reason is the conference title games.
A $2 million pledge became roughly $6 million, and that gap shows how youth sports roll-ups are underwriting their facilities.
The clearest answer to who pays for NFL games abroad sits in a regional budget line. The Comunidad de Madrid approved 1.5 million euros to sponsor the Falcons and Bengals game at the Bernabéu.

Most youth basketball operators put their energy into the gym. The parent experience around it, from registration to payment to communication, often sits on rented tools the operator does not control.
Two of Nike's most prominent athletes are backing a youth basketball league scheduled to compete with Nike's own grassroots circuit.
The WTA looked at an 80 percent share of its own future and decided to keep the risk instead.
Snapp is building a sports analytics company on the one audience that is already paying attention to every line move: people trading on outcomes.
The warning in the Montréal sale is the Vancouver one: a club can draw more than 100 interested groups and still not get a viable offer.
WTGL's first prize pool carries a number that may be harder to change than any contract: $11 million.
Choosing a college program used to run on campus visits and gut feel. Tosch.ai is betting that the transfer portal and NIL have made that expensive enough to justify a Bloomberg style data product.
A $3,000 rink in a parking garage may be the best return on capital in youth sports travel this year.
The $180 million headline on the Sina Sports Complex is the full vision, and the first hire shows who the developer wants running it.
PlayMetrics is shrinking its portfolio at the same time it is buying the platform that defines it, and eCamps Sports Network is the latest piece to leave.
Record books are one of the oldest stat products in college sports, and FanWord is trying to turn them into a live feed.
Gotham FC is being priced on what its next stadium could do, not on what its current one does.
Ricky Rubio is about to be a shareholder in the club that signs his paychecks, and the buyer behind the deal is a former Euroleague CEO.
Under Armour is pairing its newest signing with a youth mental health platform, and the structure shows how brands are trying to earn a place in school sports.
Unrivaled Basketball has found a second place to sell sponsorship: not the league, but the individual club.
Prediction market operators keep landing on the same next product: a mystery pack with a real card inside.
The Atlanta Dream outgrew their building so fast that a scheduling conflict in the WNBA Finals became the clearest argument for owning the next one.
Marc Lasry wants the market to know his Las Vegas NBA bid is alive, and the fight comes down to one number.
The expensive part of sports tracking data used to be the stadium. Stats Perform is making the case that it can be a video feed and a GPU.

When a government-owned bank puts capital behind an American sports fund, the signal is bigger than the check. Japan appears to be inviting private equity into a sports market that has been run by corporate parents for decades.
The most interesting detail in OnSport AI's $2 million pre-seed is who wrote the checks: people who own basketball teams, the exact customers for a tool that protects player availability.
The most valuable asset in American Olympic sport comes back to its owner after the 2028 Games, and the owner appears to be preparing to sell part of it.
The Arnold Palmer name is being used to roll up junior golf, and a youth sports investor with a full ladder of holdings has now bought in.
Horse racing has run on tracks, breeders and bettors for a century. The Horse Racing League is trying to run on the Formula 1 playbook instead, and its early hiring shows it.
Applications for the PEAKCONF | SportsTech Conference Startup World Cup 2027 close on Monday, November 9, and the first qualifier follows on Thursday, November 19.
A 57% EBITDA margin is the number that explains why a Swiss sports rights business is taking the reverse merger route to the stock market.
Sport has plenty of fintech apps. It does not yet have a bank, and SPORTA is hiring like a company that wants to become one.
Sports media rights are about to do something that surprises people who only follow the growth headlines: shrink.
FIFA elections are decided by 211 federations, and the Gianni Infantino challenge now has the first candidate with the profile to test that arithmetic.
The most valuable part of the Liverpool deal may be what the buyers have not bought yet.
Flag football's Olympic pitch has a gap in the middle: plenty of girls play at the youth level and the LA28 roster is coming, but college sports has had almost nowhere for them to go in between.
Moving tens of thousands of fans across a city on one night is a data problem, and UEFA is looking for founders who can solve it.
The next big retail test for a performance wearable is a beauty aisle, and the customer Whoop is chasing there is not an athlete.
Baseball is heading toward a lockout, and one of its most profitable side businesses is built to keep running through it.
Project B has now announced 28 women's players for a season that has not started. The roster is doing the work that a balance sheet cannot.
Retailers sell other companies' athletes all day. DICK'S Sporting Goods has now hired one of its own, and it chose the face of women's basketball to be the first.
Three years ago a spot in the NWSL cost $53 million. The last one sold for $205 million, and the league is about to put the next two up for bid.
A draw ceremony is usually the quietest event on a tennis calendar. The WTA has handed one to TikTok, and that choice says plenty about where it wants its next audience.
American Express is taking a card that already owns the arena entrance and putting it on a passport.
Bilt built a rewards business on rent day. It is now paying $300 million to own game day.
Cadillac has not turned a wheel in anger for a full season, and its owner is already testing what the market will pay for the privilege of being on the grid.
Sports tech founders have three chances this winter to earn a live pitch slot in Las Vegas.
There has been a lot of interest around creator-led live sports broadcasts.
The new competition for the Friday night bar tab is a 5K with a DJ set at the finish line.
The most revealing number in the Lakers sale is not $12.5 billion. It is $250 million, the reported entry ticket for the investors now being invited in.
Providence Equity is quietly assembling a pan-European budget gym empire, and Fitness Park is the piece that makes it large enough to matter.
Kimi Antonelli collected the trophy in Mexico City, but the bigger number in the Mercedes garage is on the income statement.
The Carolina Panthers are not renovating a stadium so much as buying a seat at the table where the NFL hands out its biggest events.
Women's sports has an equipment problem that capital is only beginning to price: most gear was built around a male body and then sized down.
Sports teams have spent a decade fighting for highlight clips. The next fight is for fictional stories set inside the building.
The women's sports boom now has a ledger, and the biggest line on it is not the ticket office.
Cinemark is testing whether a Cowboys game can fill a movie theater on a Monday night.
Mumbai Indians are now valued above MLB's Detroit Tigers and the NHL's Vancouver Canucks, and the way the IPL shares its money is a big part of why.
Phoenix's first Women's Final Four delivered about one-sixth of the economic impact of its last Men's Final Four, and about one-fifth of the crowd.
The PWHL has replaced its cheapest roster spots with full-time jobs.
DAZN's biggest financial safety net is a letter its own directors say is not legally binding.
The Wilf family is backing a company that books the court rental, the lesson and the youth program, and treating it as sports infrastructure.
The most valuable thing about Texas's Bevo Lab may be who gets to work in it.
The Australian Open's venture arm has found a startup that sells to the people who run ticket offices, not to the players on the court.
Most startup programs in sports ask founders for equity or a fixed calendar. Duets is launching with neither.
One billion dollars is a modest number in AI investing, which is why the people behind this partnership matter more than the pool.
Since April, GEICO has moved up the women's basketball stack one layer at a time, and Unrivaled is the top one.
Curling's business case is built on one decision made in 2024: buy the media rights, not rent a seat in someone else's broadcast.
An NIL conference that drew 230 athletes in June is becoming a year-round business, and the buyer is an NIL platform company.
Everyone in youth sports agrees coaching is the #1 reason kids stay or quit. Almost nobody measures it.
Cricket Australia is trying to sell the Big Bash to investors while the product is at its strongest.
The 2027 Africa Cup of Nations is heading to free television, and CAF appears to be betting that reach is worth more than a single large rights check.
The safest collateral in Brazilian football is not a player or a shirt sponsor. It is the money that fans pay at the turnstile.
In most clubs, a minority investor funds the dream and a majority owner decides how to spend it. LaLiga's rulebook narrows that gap.
A Manhattan bar bought insurance on a Knicks win, and the company that wants to price that insurance for everyone else has recently raised money.
Hockey started 2022 with an average franchise worth about $1 billion, and Sportico's numbers show it has outgrown every other major US league since.
LIV Golf has hired the executive who took TaylorMade from $300 million to more than $1.85 billion in sales, and the clock on its relaunch is short.

RacePace, a Vienna-based company that builds pacing, fueling and hydration plans for trail runners, is exploring a partnership with Sydney-based Minimis to put race guidance inside the field of view of Minimis Flow glasses.
Baseball's most patient audience strategy is aimed at viewers who cannot yet drive, buy tickets or hold a credit card.
The NIL money fight is moving from the football stadium to the gym floor and the sand court.
A cricket media company went from $44,318 of quarterly revenue to roughly $6.2 million in a single quarter, and the reason is a calendar, not a trend.
Olympic sports with small marketing budgets are testing a cheaper way to find fans: hand the sword to someone who already has an audience.
MGM Resorts did not buy a padel sponsorship. It bought a seat in front of the audience already in Las Vegas that week.
Sports M&A posted a record year, and the clubs are not the main story.
Portland has the women's sports credentials to host the 2031 Women's World Cup. What it lacks is a stadium that meets FIFA's terms.
The most interesting thing in sports media right now is not a new league deal. It is a guy calling games into a phone.
In sponsorship, a long relationship can work like a right of first refusal even when no contract says so. State Farm and Overtime offer a fresh example.
The first Women's Club World Cup has a host, a date, and an unresolved fight over the calendar.
Adobe's first Formula One deal includes a product that has nothing to do with fans at the track: a tool that tracks how a team shows up in AI chatbot answers.
UEFA and UK & Ireland 2028 are putting up to 200,000 pounds behind innovators with tools that leave something lasting for EURO 2028 volunteers and communities.
Two Circles puts the value of fandom at 1.94 trillion dollars, and the more useful number in its new report is the growth rate, not the total.

Sports tracking has always been priced by the camera. The more cameras a system needs, and the more precisely they must be calibrated, the fewer venues can afford it. NVIDIA's latest sports release goes after that cost.

When the CEO of one of the world's largest toy companies says trading cards are now the biggest category in toys and games, the sports collectibles boom stops looking like a hobby story and starts looking like a retail one.
College basketball programs now run closer to a small talent business than a traditional roster operation, and the software behind that business is becoming a competitive question of its own.
The NBA is no longer pitching European clubs on basketball. It is pitching them on a faster path to a profit.
Sports rights are getting bigger and each match is worth less, which is the backdrop for the sports tech market's steady growth.
A sitcom about a sports news show that ABC canceled in 2000 still teaches more about sports media than most conference panels.
Russell Wilson's first big post-retirement business move is not another apparel line. It is a bet on a wearable with no subscription.
Voice is turning into a sports media layer, and four deployments from one vendor show the different shapes it can take.
